title: Weekly cisplatin + nasopharyngeal radiotherapy
context_label: Chemoradiation for locally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
indication_text: Chemoradiation for locally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
purpose: Weekly cisplatin is given alongside radiotherapy for cancer of the nasopharynx, the space behind the nose. This information covers the concurrent treatment phase; any chemotherapy before or after it has a separate plan.
schedule_summary: Cisplatin 40 mg/m² once a week for six planned doses during radiotherapy. Cisplatin is given before radiation on the same day. If radiotherapy is cancelled, cisplatin is held until radiation resumes; the team updates both calendars.
administration_text: Cisplatin 40 mg/m² is infused over 1 hour, with prescribed fluids before and after, mineral replacement and anti-sickness medicines. Allow additional time for review, hydration and the same-day radiation appointment.
monitoring_summary: Blood count, kidney and liver function; audiology and measured creatinine clearance when indicated. Review hearing, tinnitus, nerve symptoms and medicines. Dental and nutrition preparation and a swallowing plan are important before head and neck radiotherapy. Blood count, kidney and liver function before every cisplatin cycle. Report hearing or tinnitus and nerve changes before each dose; audiology is repeated when indicated. Review weight, drinking, swallowing, mouth and skin symptoms during the radiation course. Follow kidney, mineral, hearing and nerve problems and continuing radiation effects. Dental, nutrition and swallowing care may remain necessary after the last dose. Scans, examinations and any thyroid or other late-effect tests are individualised by the radiation and oncology teams; no universal scan or blood tumour-marker schedule is specified here.

agents.name: Cisplatin
agents.explanation: Cisplatin forms links in DNA that make it harder for cells to repair and divide. During chemoradiation it also increases the effect of radiotherapy. Healthy cells can be affected, which is why kidney, blood, hearing and nerve checks matter.
agents.watch: Report reduced urine, persistent vomiting, tinnitus, hearing change or new tingling.
risks: Low blood counts and serious infection
Hearing loss or tinnitus, which can persist
Infusion reaction and effects on fertility

agents.name: Radiotherapy
agents.mechanism: Damages cancer cells in the planned treatment area
agents.explanation: Radiotherapy directs radiation at a carefully planned area. It is delivered on its own appointment calendar. Effects depend on which tissues receive radiation and can build up during the course or continue after it finishes.
agents.watch: Report difficulty swallowing, weight loss, mouth pain, skin breakdown or problems managing saliva.
risks: Dry mouth, taste and saliva changes
Skin reaction in the treated area
Some swallowing, saliva or tissue effects can be lasting

support.title: One written medicine plan
support.text: Ask for one schedule showing prevention medicines, rescue treatment and what to do if symptoms persist. Do not add, double or restart medicines from an old prescription.

support.title: Hydration and kidney protection
support.text: Cisplatin needs prescribed fluids before and after infusion. Follow the team’s drinking advice and report much less urine, vomiting or inability to drink. Do not change fluid intake or diuretics without advice.

support.title: Food, fluids and weight
support.text: A dietitian can tailor food texture, supplements and calorie or protein needs. Tell the team early if eating or drinking becomes difficult; do not wait for substantial weight loss. Fluid targets depend on kidney and heart health.

support.title: Oral and dental care
support.text: Use the mouth-care plan provided by the team and tell them about ulcers, thrush, bleeding or pain. Inform your dentist about cancer treatment. Before any dental procedure, confirm timing with the oncology team.

support.title: Swallowing and communication
support.text: A speech and language therapist can assess swallowing and advise exercises or safer food and drink textures. Follow the individual assessment; a general guide cannot decide which textures are safe for you.

support.title: Fertility, pregnancy and medicines
support.text: Discuss fertility and pregnancy precautions before treatment and the medicine-specific duration of contraception afterwards. Ask about breastfeeding. Bring a full medicine, supplement and allergy list; check before adding over-the-counter or herbal products.

sections.title: Before the first visit
sections.text: Confirm the exact regimen, treatment aim, baseline tests, transport, support medicines and actual urgent contact numbers. Bring any hearing concerns, swallowing problems and medicine list.

sections.title: Time in the unit
sections.text: Cisplatin is given by IV infusion with fluids before and after, prescribed mineral replacement and anti-sickness medicines. The unit confirms infusion and hydration times and checks that radiotherapy is proceeding that day. Allow time for both departments.

sections.title: Two departments, one calendar
sections.text: Radiation appointments are separate from medicine visits. Keep one calendar showing both departments and tests; tell the team promptly about a cancelled session.

sections.title: Practical help
sections.text: Tell the team about travel, cost, work, caring responsibilities, communication or reading needs. Ask whether a support person or interpreter can attend and how treatment changes will be explained.

sections.title: Leaving the unit
sections.text: Check the next visit and blood-test dates, support medicines and who to call if unwell. Have the team replace example phone numbers before using the wallet card.

chapters.title: Understanding your diagnosis
chapters.intro: Keep your pathology and agreed treatment goal with your records.

items.title: Site, type and stage
items.text: Nasopharyngeal cancer starts behind the nose. Ask about the pathology, stage and any tumour tests relevant to your own plan. This is a different pathway from squamous cancer at other head and neck sites.

items.title: Which pathway applies?
items.text: Chemoradiation for locally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma. This guide should match the named treatment on your prescription.

items.title: What tumour tests mean
items.text: Your team explains any HPV/p16, Epstein–Barr virus or other tumour tests relevant to your cancer site. Not every head and neck cancer needs the same tests; the medicine safety checks are a separate matter.

chapters.title: Treatment choices and your priorities
chapters.intro: The consent conversation explains the boundaries of the plan.

items.title: Benefit and alternatives
items.text: Weekly cisplatin is given alongside radiotherapy for cancer of the nasopharynx, the space behind the nose. This information covers the concurrent treatment phase; any chemotherapy before or after it has a separate plan. Ask how alternatives compare for your health, goals and previous treatment. A study result cannot predict an individual outcome.

items.title: A pause is a treatment decision
items.text: The clinician may delay, change or stop treatment because of symptoms, test results or your priorities. Record which component is affected and what is needed before restarting. Do not restart from an old prescription.

items.title: Combining treatment approaches
items.text: Radiotherapy treats a planned local area while medicine supports the cancer treatment. The radiation prescription, number of sessions and late-effect plan are agreed separately.

chapters.title: Preparing for and receiving treatment
chapters.intro: Plan the appointments and support around the prescribed schedule.

items.title: Your first visit
items.text: Cisplatin is given by IV infusion with fluids before and after, prescribed mineral replacement and anti-sickness medicines. The unit confirms infusion and hydration times and checks that radiotherapy is proceeding that day. Allow time for both departments.

items.title: If an appointment changes
items.text: If radiation is cancelled, cisplatin is withheld until radiation resumes. Ask both departments to confirm revised dates; do not assume the chemotherapy visit proceeds unchanged.

items.title: What the record shows
items.text: Write the actual treatment date, phase and any change. The wallet card is a brief record; the passport holds the fuller history. It does not replace the hospital treatment record.

chapters.title: Between visits: symptoms and medicines
chapters.intro: Use the agreed home plan and contact pathway.

items.title: Symptoms have no fixed calendar
items.text: Some effects appear soon after treatment and others build over weeks. Do not wait for the next appointment if a symptom is new, severe or worsening.

items.title: A medicine plan you can use
items.text: Keep prevention, rescue and regular medicines clearly separated on one written list. Record what you have taken and the response, so the team can adjust it. Do not double a missed dose unless your prescriber tells you to.

items.title: When self-care is not enough
items.text: Contact oncology promptly for fever, sudden illness, persistent vomiting, much less urine, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Report hearing change, ringing in the ears or new numbness before the next dose. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain or collapse is an emergency.

chapters.title: Mouth, teeth and jaw care
chapters.intro: Dental preparation and gentle daily care reduce avoidable problems.

items.title: Before treatment
items.text: Arrange dental assessment before head and neck radiation. The dental and oncology teams decide what treatment is needed and how much healing time is required; do not schedule extractions independently.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: Follow the prescribed brushing, fluoride, rinse and pain-relief advice. Report ulcers, infection, new bleeding, difficulty wearing dentures or worsening jaw opening. Avoid starting a new mouthwash without checking if the mouth is sore.

items.title: After head and neck radiation
items.text: Dry mouth can increase dental problems and some radiation effects last. Keep regular dental care and tell any future dentist that you have had head and neck radiation before invasive treatment. Your radiation/dental team plans any procedure.

chapters.title: Eating, drinking and maintaining strength
chapters.intro: The aim is adequate intake and comfort during treatment.

items.title: Recognising an intake problem
items.text: Record weight and report food or drink becoming harder to manage. Pain, taste change, dry mouth or nausea can each need a different response; a dietitian can adapt the plan to you.

items.title: If ordinary food is not enough
items.text: The team may suggest food fortification, supplements or tube feeding when intake or swallowing safety requires it. A tube is a support option, not a judgement about how well you have tried to eat. Training and follow-up are needed.

items.title: Fluid needs are individual
items.text: Ask for a realistic drinking plan that accounts for kidney/heart problems and any feeding tube. Persistent vomiting, dizziness, markedly reduced urine or inability to drink needs urgent contact.

chapters.title: Swallowing, voice and communication
chapters.intro: A speech and language therapist can help protect function.

items.title: Swallowing assessment
items.text: Report coughing or choking with food or drink, a wet-sounding voice after swallowing, food sticking or repeated chest infections. The team may need to assess aspiration risk and safe textures.

items.title: Exercises and rehabilitation
items.text: Do swallowing or jaw exercises only as taught for your situation. Treatment and recovery can change what is comfortable and safe. Ask for reassessment when symptoms change.

items.title: Communication needs
items.text: Tell the team about changes in speech, voice or hearing. Ask for written instructions, communication aids, an interpreter or help involving a support person.

chapters.title: Daily life and emotional support
chapters.intro: Practical adjustments can make the plan easier to follow.

items.title: Energy and activity
items.text: Balance rest with manageable activity according to your ability and team advice. Ask for help if weakness, falls, sleep difficulty or pain interferes with daily life.

items.title: Smoking and alcohol
items.text: Ask for support to stop smoking and discuss alcohol with the team. Mouth irritation, medicine interactions and head and neck recovery can change what is safe for you.

items.title: Emotional and practical concerns
items.text: Tell the team about anxiety, appearance or intimacy concerns, finances, travel and caring responsibilities. Ask which local supports are available; resources can be added to your record when confirmed.

chapters.title: Recovery, assessment and longer-term care
chapters.intro: Treatment completion and recovery are different milestones.

items.title: Continuing symptoms
items.text: Follow kidney, mineral, hearing and nerve problems and continuing radiation effects. Dental, nutrition and swallowing care may remain necessary after the last dose. Scans, examinations and any thyroid or other late-effect tests are individualised by the radiation and oncology teams; no universal scan or blood tumour-marker schedule is specified here.

items.title: Cancer assessment
items.text: Your team sets examinations and imaging around the disease, treatment and symptoms. Record who arranges each test and who explains the result. An unbooked scan is not automatically due at a fixed week because a general guide says so.

items.title: Information for other clinicians
items.text: Keep the regimen name, last treatment date, ongoing medicines and relevant alert card. Tell clinicians about earlier immune treatment or head and neck radiation even after the course has ended.

chapters.title: Your records and additional help
chapters.intro: Keep essential instructions available on paper.

items.title: The passport and wallet card
items.text: The three-page companion gives the essentials. Use the passport for the agreed plan, visits, test results, symptoms and questions. The wallet QR opens this exact treatment’s further information; it contains no personal clinical record.

items.title: Contacts before patient use
items.text: The phone numbers printed as examples must be replaced and checked by the treating service. Add the unit’s daytime, out-of-hours and backup route; keep this information where you and a support person can find it.

items.title: If you prefer paper
items.text: Use the full printable handbook in its chapter order and write questions in the passport. You do not need to scan the QR or follow an internet link to use the essential treatment and safety information.

evidence.title: Understanding the evidence
evidence.intro: Cisplatin is used with radiotherapy under the exact NCCP indication and schedule.
evidence.population: Chemoradiation for locally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
evidence.comparison: Evidence must match cancer site, whether treatment is definitive or postoperative, and the cisplatin schedule.
evidence.interpretation: The NCCP-cited Chan trial studied weekly cisplatin 40 mg/m² with radiation in nasopharyngeal carcinoma and reported a survival advantage over radiation alone in that historical population. It is distinct from the evidence for squamous cancer elsewhere in the head and neck. The current NCCP schedule governs the six-dose plan; the trial does not define an individual prognosis.
limitations: Cisplatin dose, treatment setting and cancer site affect applicability.
No survival figure from a different regimen or disease is presented as the benefit of this treatment.

consent_support: Discuss the individual aim, alternatives and uncertainty; serious or lasting harms; treatment burden; fertility and pregnancy precautions; and the patient’s priorities. Explain blood-count suppression/infection, nausea, kidney/mineral injury, hearing loss and neuropathy that can persist, hydration and same-day radiation coordination. Discuss radiation mouth, skin, swallowing, saliva, dental and jaw effects, including lasting effects and potential nutritional support. Radiation has its own consent process. Confirm actual urgent contacts and teach-back; this draft does not authorise treatment.
